steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a software engineering paper on testing deep neural networks. It should contrast testing aimed at finding mispredictions with operational testing aimed at estimating accuracy, introduce our method DeepEST that tries to do both, summarise the experiments, and end with the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- DNNs in safety-critical systems; why testing them matters
- Current DNN testing research: finding mispredictions, coverage criteria
- Problem: failure-finding testing does not tell us the accuracy in operation
- Operational testing for accuracy estimation; existing approach and its limit
- Our proposal: DeepEST, and how it compares to both strategies
- Experiments and results
- Paper structure

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep Neural Networks (DNN) are now part of many applications, and this includes safety-critical software systems, for example in the medical domain and in autonomous driving. Testing is a very important activity in the development of these systems. It matters for quality and safety reasons, because we want to avoid catastrophic failures caused by the DNN, and it matters for cost too, since very large samples may be needed to test a DNN reliably.

There is a lot of research effort at the moment on DNN testing. The main goal is to find adversarial examples that cause mispredictions, that is to expose as many failing behaviours as possible. Several structural coverage criteria were proposed to drive the automated generation of test inputs and to assess test adequacy, such as neuron coverage, k-multisection neuron coverage, neuron boundary coverage and combinatorial coverage. Some have argued that these criteria can be misleading, since the number of misclassified inputs in a test set has a low correlation with its coverage. Recently Wu et al. and Kim et al. looked at discrepancy measures between the training/validation data and the test data, to improve fault detection and to get coverage criteria that are better correlated to inputs that induce failures.

What comes out of this kind of failure-finding testing (and then debugging) is an improved DNN with a higher accuracy. This is similar to what is called debug testing in the traditional testing literature. Testing DNN-based software is different from testing conventional software in some ways (e.g., how the oracle is defined), which makes DNN testing problematic. But there is also another issue, which is that the testing results obtained this way are not necessarily related to the accuracy that is actually experienced in operation. The testing data may not be representative of the actual operational context. This can happen when the test data are generated artificially (like when adversarial examples are generated) or when they are very different from the input observed in the field. So the number of mispredictions and/or the coverage achieved only give an “indirect” measure of the expected accuracy in operation, which for the reasons above is also inaccurate, and in the end also of the confidence we can put in the DNN.

A research path that is less investigated is to test a DNN with the explicit goal of getting a statistical estimate of its expected accuracy in the operational context. In software reliability engineering this is a well established practice, called operational testing. The objective is to assess how well a DNN will perform in the context it is intended for, using a small but effective amount of test data. If testers have a cost-effective accuracy estimate, they can set a threshold-based release criterion and correct or tune their networks (e.g., adjust the DNN structure or hyper-parameters) until the criterion is met. The reference scenario is this one. A DNN model is trained with a set of data (training dataset) and it is meant to operate in a given context (operational context). For testing the model there is an arbitrarily large set of operational data available (operational dataset) with examples whose correct label is unknown. The tester has to select a small subset of the operational data, which is labelled manually and used as test cases to estimate the accuracy of the model in operation. Because labelling is manual, testers usually look for a trade-off between a good estimate and the labelling cost. Li et al. have recently faced this problem. Their selection criterion minimises the cross-entropy between the selected test data and the whole set of unlabelled operational data, so that the sample of tests is representative of the operational context. This approach does not look explicitly for failing examples, so it does not leave much room for improving the DNN accuracy. Seen this way, many of the selected tests are useless, because they are non-failing examples which only serve to have highly-confident estimates.

- DeepEST
  - either failures but not representative (adversarial-like) or representative but few failures (operational); target both drawbacks
  - DeepEST (Deep neural networks Enhanced Sampler for operational Testing): operational testing method for DNN
  - test suites from operational dataset: close and efficient accuracy estimate + high number of failing examples
  - paraphrase O. Wilde: “Experience is the hardest kind of teacher. It gives you the test first and the lesson afterward.” -> sample many failing tests to learn from while building tests for accuracy estimate
  - vs pure operational testing: more precise and efficient estimates (number of tests) + debug-testing-like scenarios (debugging/re-training)
  - vs adversarial-like testing: accuracy estimates -> evaluate alternative designs, fine tuning, release criterion related to operation
- Experiments
  - various DNN and datasets: effectiveness, sensitivity to number of tests selected, dependency on dataset
  - four variants (auxiliary information)
  - estimates similar to state-of-the-art; 5 to 30 times more mispredictions, same sample size
- Structure: II concepts; III algorithm; IV-V experimentation; VI related work; VII conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep Neural Networks (DNN) are now part of many applications, and this includes safety-critical software systems, for example in the medical domain and in autonomous driving. Testing is a very important activity in the development of these systems. It matters for quality and safety reasons, because we want to avoid catastrophic failures caused by the DNN, and it matters for cost too, since very large samples may be needed to test a DNN reliably.

There is a lot of research effort at the moment on DNN testing. The main goal is to find adversarial examples that cause mispredictions, that is to expose as many failing behaviours as possible. Several structural coverage criteria were proposed to drive the automated generation of test inputs and to assess test adequacy, such as neuron coverage, k-multisection neuron coverage, neuron boundary coverage and combinatorial coverage. Some have argued that these criteria can be misleading, since the number of misclassified inputs in a test set has a low correlation with its coverage. Recently Wu et al. and Kim et al. looked at discrepancy measures between the training/validation data and the test data, to improve fault detection and to get coverage criteria that are better correlated to inputs that induce failures.

What comes out of this kind of failure-finding testing (and then debugging) is an improved DNN with a higher accuracy. This is similar to what is called debug testing in the traditional testing literature. Testing DNN-based software is different from testing conventional software in some ways (e.g., how the oracle is defined), which makes DNN testing problematic. But there is also another issue, which is that the testing results obtained this way are not necessarily related to the accuracy that is actually experienced in operation. The testing data may not be representative of the actual operational context. This can happen when the test data are generated artificially (like when adversarial examples are generated) or when they are very different from the input observed in the field. So the number of mispredictions and/or the coverage achieved only give an “indirect” measure of the expected accuracy in operation, which for the reasons above is also inaccurate, and in the end also of the confidence we can put in the DNN.

A research path that is less investigated is to test a DNN with the explicit goal of getting a statistical estimate of its expected accuracy in the operational context. In software reliability engineering this is a well established practice, called operational testing. The objective is to assess how well a DNN will perform in the context it is intended for, using a small but effective amount of test data. If testers have a cost-effective accuracy estimate, they can set a threshold-based release criterion and correct or tune their networks (e.g., adjust the DNN structure or hyper-parameters) until the criterion is met. The reference scenario is this one. A DNN model is trained with a set of data (training dataset) and it is meant to operate in a given context (operational context). For testing the model there is an arbitrarily large set of operational data available (operational dataset) with examples whose correct label is unknown. The tester has to select a small subset of the operational data, which is labelled manually and used as test cases to estimate the accuracy of the model in operation. Because labelling is manual, testers usually look for a trade-off between a good estimate and the labelling cost. Li et al. have recently faced this problem. Their selection criterion minimises the cross-entropy between the selected test data and the whole set of unlabelled operational data, so that the sample of tests is representative of the operational context. This approach does not look explicitly for failing examples, so it does not leave much room for improving the DNN accuracy. Seen this way, many of the selected tests are useless, because they are non-failing examples which only serve to have highly-confident estimates.

So we either have a test suite that exposes failures but is not representative (adversarial-like testing), or tests that are representative but expose few failures (operational testing). In this paper we target the drawbacks of both strategies together. We present DeepEST (Deep neural networks Enhanced Sampler for operational Testing), which is an operational testing method for DNN. It builds test suites from an operational dataset in order to give a close and efficient estimate of the expected accuracy and at the same time to find a high number of failing examples. To paraphrase a famous aphorism by O. Wilde (“Experience is the hardest kind of teacher. It gives you the test first and the lesson afterward.”), DeepEST aims to sample many failing tests to learn from out of the operational data, while building a set of tests that is suited for estimating the DNN accuracy.

Compared to pure operational testing, DeepEST is expected to give DNN accuracy estimates that are more precise and more efficient (in terms of number of tests required), and it also has the practical advantage of enabling scenarios like debug testing (improving the accuracy through debugging/re-training). Compared to adversarial-like testing, DeepEST gives accuracy estimates, which makes it possible to evaluate alternative designs or fine tune the DNN, and to set a release criterion that is directly related to what will be observed in operation.

We present experiments with various DNN and datasets, which assess the effectiveness of DeepEST, its sensitivity to the number of tests selected from the operational dataset, and its dependency on the dataset. DeepEST can exploit various types of auxiliary information to select tests, so the experimental study considers four variants. The results show that all the variants give accuracy estimates that are similar to the ones of the state-of-the-art technique, while detecting from 5 to 30 times more mispredictions with the same sample size.

The paper is structured as follows. Section II introduces the sampling-based operational testing concepts that DeepEST uses. Section III describes the DeepEST algorithm. Sections IV and V report the experimentation. Section VI discusses related work. Section VII concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep Neural Networks (DNN) are today integral part of many applications, including safety-critical software systems such as in the medical [1] and autonomous driving domains [2]. Testing is a crucial activity in the development of such systems, both for quality/safety reasons, to avoid DNN-caused catastrophic failures [3,4], and for cost – very large samples may be needed to reliably test a DNN [5,6].

A significant research effort is currently being put on DNN testing. A primary goal is to find adversarial examples causing mispredictions, namely to expose as many failing behaviours as possible [7,8,9,10,11]. Several structural coverage criteria have been proposed to drive the automated generation of test inputs and to assess test adequacy – neuron coverage [7], k-multisection neuron coverage, neuron boundary coverage [8], combinatorial coverage [10]. It has been argued that these criteria may be misleading, because of the low correlation between the number of misclassified inputs in a test set and its coverage [12]. Wu et al. [13] and Kim et al. [14] recently considered discrepancy measures between the training/validation data and the test data, to improve fault detection and to obtain coverage criteria better correlated to failure-inducing inputs.

The output of this type of failure-finding testing (and then debugging) process is an improved DNN, with higher accuracy. This resembles what is called debug testing in the traditional testing literature [15]. Beside differences between testing DNN-based and conventional software (e.g., the oracle definition), which make DNN testing problematic, a further issue is that the testing results obtained this way are not necessarily related to the accuracy actually experienced in operation. In fact, testing data may be not representative of the actual operational context. This may happen when test data are generated artificially (like in adversarial examples generation) or when they differ significantly from the input observed in the field. The number of mispredictions and/or the coverage achieved give only an “indirect” (and, for what said, inaccurate) measure of the expected accuracy in operation, and ultimately of the confidence that can be placed in the DNN.

A less investigated research path is testing a DNN with the explicit goal of providing a statistical estimate of its expected accuracy in the operational context. In software reliability engineering, this is a well established practice known as operational testing [16]. The objective is to assess how well a DNN will perform in the intended context using a small yet effective amount of test data. With a cost-effective accuracy estimate, testers can establish a threshold-based release criterion and correct or tune their networks (e.g., adjust the DNN structure or hyper-parameters) until the criterion is met. The reference scenario is the following: a DNN model is trained with a set of data (training dataset) and is meant to operate in a given context (operational context). To test the model, an arbitrarily large set of operational data is available (operational dataset), containing examples whose correct label is unknown: the tester's goal is to select a small subset of the operational data, to be manually labelled and used as test cases to estimate the accuracy of the model in operation. Due to manual labelling, testers typically look for a trade-off between a good estimate and the labelling cost. This problem has recently been faced by Li et al. [17]. Their selection criterion is to minimise the cross-entropy between the selected test data and the whole set of unlabelled operational data, so as to have a sample of tests representative of the operational context. As this approach does not explicitly look for failing examples, it does not give much room for improving the DNN accuracy. From this viewpoint, many of the selected tests are useless, as they are non-failing examples that only serve the purpose of having highly-confident estimates.

Given the above, we either have a test suite exposing failures but not representative (adversarial-like testing), or representative tests but few failures exposed (operational testing). This paper targets the drawbacks of both strategies together. We present DeepEST (Deep neural networks Enhanced Sampler for operational Testing), an operational testing method for DNN that builds test suites from an operational dataset so as to provide a close and efficient estimate of the expected accuracy and, at the same time, to find a high number of failing examples. Paraphrasing a famous aphorism by O. Wilde (“Experience is the hardest kind of teacher. It gives you the test first and the lesson afterward.”), DeepEST aims to sample many failing tests to learn from out of the operational data, while building a set of tests suited for the DNN accuracy estimate.

With respect to pure operational testing, DeepEST is expected to provide DNN accuracy estimates that are more precise and more efficient (in number of tests required), plus the practical advantage of enabling debug-testing-like scenarios (improving accuracy through debugging/re-training). With respect to adversarial-like testing, DeepEST provides accuracy estimates, enabling the evaluation of alternative designs or DNN fine tuning, and a release criterion directly related to what will be observed in operation.

Experiments with various DNN and datasets are presented, assessing DeepEST effectiveness, its sensitivity to the number of tests selected from the operational dataset, and its dependency on the dataset. Since DeepEST can exploit various types of auxiliary information to select tests, the experimental study considers four variants. The results show that all the variants produce accuracy estimates similar to those of the state-of-the-art technique, while detecting from 5 to 30 times more mispredictions with the same sample size.

The paper is structured as follows. Section II introduces the sampling-based operational testing concepts used by DeepEST. Section III describes the DeepEST algorithm. Sections IV and V report the experimentation. Section VI discusses related work. Section VII concludes the paper.
